entry.title: A population-register study finds no robust young-worker employment displacement in Norway and flags pre-trend contamination. The U.S. entry warning remains, but it cannot be treated as a universal AI verdict.

A firm-data study of recorded AI spending reports headcount growth among selected heavy U.S. adopters. It separates actual adoption from occupational exposure but does not settle the early-career risk signal or prove cause.

A revised Stanford payroll analysis raises the early-career warning to a 19% relative gap, while a new cross-country study makes remote work a concrete rival explanation. The answer is stronger on risk and stricter on cause.

A new Census graduate study strengthens the U.S. early-career warning with initial employment and earnings outcomes, while broad job-posting research still finds no distinct AI-driven decline. The answer is now sharper and more bounded.

First public evidence map: early-career hiring is the sharpest U.S. warning, but its AI attribution is unresolved; firm reports and Danish records show task change without a common wage-or-hours result.
